strengths: Clear motivation addressing a well-known open challenge in class-pose decomposition and geometric deep learning: overcoming the arbitrary orientation of learned canonical reference frames to uncover true, interpretable symmetry distributions.

Sound mathematical foundation: Proposition 3.1 and the proof in Appendix B provide a clear theoretical justification for canonical orientation normalization via the Fréchet mean on Lie groups, guaranteeing convergence in Wasserstein distance.

First extension of instance-specific symmetry discovery to continuous 3D transformations ($SO(3)$) on large-scale molecular conformation data (GEOM-QM9), moving significantly beyond standard 2D image rotations.

Intuitive qualitative behavior demonstrated on distinct classes related by group transformations (e.g., distinguishing '6' and '9' while recovering their respective natural canonical poses and shared symmetry profiles), alongside practical utility shown in out-of-distribution pose detection.
weaknesses: Lack of quantitative comparisons against baselines: While qualitative differences with IE-AE and SGM are highlighted, the paper does not quantitatively benchmark RECON against competing methods (e.g., SGM [Allingham et al., 2024], VP G-CNNs [Kim et al., 2024]) on symmetry parameter error, canonical alignment consistency, or OOD pose detection.

Reliance on synthetic rotation distributions: The experimental evaluations on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and GEOM-QM9 rely on artificially injected group transformations (uniform/Gaussian on $SO(2)$ and synthetic matrix-Fisher rotations on $SO(3)$). Demonstrating performance on naturally occurring, uncurated pose variations or physical symmetries would substantially strengthen the empirical claims.

Multi-stage training complexity and parametric assumptions: The overall pipeline is multi-stage (training the IE-AE backbone, performing k-NN neighborhood retrieval in latent space $\mathcal{Z}$, calculating empirical Fréchet means and fitting distribution parameters, and subsequently training inference networks $\Theta$ and $\Lambda$). Furthermore, the downstream inference of distribution parameters $\Theta(x)$ assumes a known parametric family (e.g., uniform, Gaussian, or matrix-Fisher).

strengths: Addresses an important and recognized shortcoming in class-pose decomposition and unsupervised symmetry discovery methods, namely the arbitrary canonical reference orientation learned during training.

Provides a sound mathematical justification (Proposition 3.1 and Appendix B) showing that right-translating by the empirical Fréchet mean recovers the identity-centered symmetry distribution in the low-noise, large-sample limit.
Successfully extends class-pose normalization and symmetry discovery beyond 2D planar rotations to continuous 3D rotations (SO(3)) on molecular graphs (GEOM/QM9) using matrix-Fisher distributions.
Demonstrates an interesting downstream application in out-of-distribution (OOD) pose detection via the predicted likelihood under the inferred symmetry distribution.
weaknesses: Lack of direct quantitative comparisons against existing symmetry-learning baselines (e.g., SGM, Augerino, Partial G-CNNs, VP G-CNNs) on standard benchmark metrics; the evaluation mostly compares RECON's predictions directly against synthetic ground truth.

The experimental validation relies entirely on synthetically injected rotation distributions (uniform/Gaussian in 2D, synthetic matrix-Fisher in 3D) rather than discovering natural, non-artificially introduced symmetries in real-world data.

The multi-stage pipeline is complex and requires several heuristic steps: training an IE-AE, performing k-NN in latent space, computing Fréchet means and moment estimators under assumed parametric families, and subsequently training two separate auxiliary networks (Theta and Lambda) on noisy pseudo-labels.

The parametric assumption in Section 3.3 (assuming known distribution families like uniform or matrix-Fisher) limits general applicability to arbitrary real-world multimodal or irregular symmetry distributions.

The definition of 'natural pose' depends strictly on the empirical Fréchet mean being the true semantic canonical. If the underlying data distribution is inherently asymmetric or skewed, the recovered canonical orientation will remain biased.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addressing the arbitrary canonical pose ambiguity in class-pose decomposition methods is an important and principled step toward discovering instance-specific, interpretable symmetry distributions.

Sound mathematical foundation: Proposition 3.1 and its proof in Appendix B clearly justify using the Fréchet mean to estimate the group offset induced by arbitrary canonicals and recovering the identity-centered distribution.

Extension to 3D transformation groups: Unlike most prior symmetry discovery works that focus strictly on 2D images, this work successfully scales the formulation to SO(3) rotations on 3D geometric molecular graphs (GEOM/QM9).

Effective downstream demonstrations: The paper demonstrates concrete practical utility, including resolving canonical collapse for transformation-related classes (e.g., digits '6' and '9') and detecting out-of-distribution poses with strong AUC-ROC metrics.
weaknesses: Synthetic pose distributions: Ground-truth symmetry distributions in both the 2D benchmarks (MNIST/FashionMNIST) and 3D graphs (GEOM) are synthetically generated via manual augmentations (uniform, Gaussian, and matrix-Fisher distributions) rather than naturally occurring asymmetric or partially symmetric real-world data distributions.

Multi-stage training pipeline with high compute cost: The workflow requires first training an equivariant autoencoder, running k-NN clustering across the latent space to calculate empirical Fréchet means and parameter estimates, and then training two additional auxiliary networks (Theta and Lambda). For 3D graphs, this requires over 7.5 days on an A100 GPU.

Reliance on parametric distribution assumptions for amortization: The amortized inference step (Section 3.3) assumes a known parametric family (such as matrix-Fisher or uniform) to compute pseudo-labels. In real-world data with arbitrary multimodal or mixed discrete-continuous symmetries, this parametric fitting may be restrictive.

Limited quantitative baseline comparisons: While qualitative comparisons with standard IE-AE and SGM canonicals are provided, the paper lacks direct quantitative baseline comparisons against competing symmetry discovery or partial equivariance approaches (e.g., SGM, VP G-CNNs) on the parameter estimation and OOD detection tasks.

strengths: Clear motivation addressing a recognized limitation of class-pose decomposition methods, namely that learned canonical poses and their induced relative pose distributions are arbitrary and training-dependent.

Sound mathematical foundation: using the Fréchet mean (and proposing a robust Tukey-Fréchet mean for multimodal settings) to normalize arbitrary canonical offsets is theoretically grounded, elegant, and architecture-agnostic.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation extending beyond standard 2D image benchmarks to complex 3D molecular graphs (SO(3) transformations on GEOM-QM9).

Effective downstream applications: RECON demonstrates solid gains in test-time canonicalization for frozen classifiers without retraining or class-label supervision, competitive with or outperforming supervised test-time methods like EquiAdapt.
weaknesses: Evaluations rely on synthetically injected rotation distributions (uniform / Gaussian on 2D images, matrix-Fisher on pre-aligned 3D conformers) rather than naturally occurring, unconstrained real-world symmetry shifts.

The pipeline is multi-staged and heavily depends on the invariant latent space quality of the underlying class-pose backbone; if the backbone exhibits severe latent overlap or collapse between distinct classes, the k-NN approximation degrades as acknowledged in Appendix D.3.

While the concept of canonical normalization via the Fréchet mean is effective, the core theoretical result (Proposition 3.1) is fairly straightforward given standard continuity and consistency assumptions on Riemannian manifolds.

strengths: Clear motivation and well-identified problem: Existing class-pose decomposition methods (such as IE-AE and SGM) suffer from learning arbitrary, out-of-distribution canonical frames, which distorts the relative pose distribution and limits interpretability and downstream transfer. RECON addresses this fundamental issue directly.

Solid theoretical foundation: Proposition 3.1 cleanly proves that the empirical Fréchet mean of relative poses converges to the canonical offset, allowing exact recovery of the centered symmetry distribution via a simple right translation. The introduction of the robust Tukey-Fréchet mean effectively resolves mode-averaging issues for multimodal pose distributions.

Validation across both 2D and 3D domains: Moving beyond typical 2D toy benchmarks to evaluate on 3D molecular conformations (GEOM-QM9 with SE(3) rotations) is commendable and demonstrates applicability to higher-dimensional Lie groups.

Demonstrated utility in practical downstream tasks: The framework demonstrates clear real-world applications in out-of-distribution (OOD) pose detection and test-time canonicalization, granting group invariance to frozen backbones without retraining.

Thorough analysis and honest limitations: The authors provide detailed investigations into neighborhood size $k$, equivalence class hit rates, failure modes under inter-class feature overlap (e.g., FashionMNIST footwear classes), and computational overhead.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on invariant representation quality: Approximating equivalence classes $[x]$ via $k$-NN in the latent space $Z$ assumes that structurally/semantically similar instances form clean clusters. When classes have ambiguous boundaries or high intra-class deformation (as observed in FashionMNIST tops/shoes), the nearest-neighbor set is corrupted, which degrades offset estimation.

Synthetic rotation distributions: While testing on GEOM-QM9 is an asset, the rotational distributions in all experiments were artificially injected (e.g., matrix-Fisher and uniform/Gaussian rotations applied post-hoc). Demonstrating symmetry discovery on naturally occurring pose distributions (such as cryo-EM particles or real-world sensor data) would make the empirical validation substantially more convincing.

Multi-stage pipeline complexity: Recovering and deploying symmetries requires training the base IE-AE, performing offline $k$-NN and Fréchet mean estimation over the entire dataset to extract pseudo-labels, and subsequently training two separate networks ($\Theta$ and $\Lambda$). While amortized at inference, this pipeline is multi-stage and introduces several hyperparameters.

Modest gains on 3D test-time canonicalization: In Figure 6d, test-time canonicalization on GEOM-QM9 yields an accuracy of 55.92% (up from 52.40% baseline), which remains far below the fully equivariant SEGNN (98.55%) and the perfect canonicalization upper bound (96.40%).

strengths: Clear problem formulation: The paper tackles an important and well-recognized drawback of class-pose disentanglement methods (such as IE-AEs and SGMs), where learned canonicals adopt arbitrary, often out-of-distribution orientations.

Sound mathematical foundation: Proposition 3.1 provides a clean theoretical justification for normalizing canonicals via the Fréchet mean of relative poses, and the Tukey-Fréchet extension effectively handles multimodal distributions that would otherwise break standard Riemannian barycenters.

Extension to 3D groups: While most symmetry discovery works restrict their empirical validation to 2D rotations or synthetic toys, this work demonstrates discovery of continuous SO(3) symmetry distributions on 3D molecular conformations (GEOM-QM9).

Practical downstream applications: Demonstrating that data-aligned canonicalization can be applied at test time to grant invariance to frozen, pre-trained models without retraining is a compelling and pragmatic contribution.
weaknesses: Reliance on synthetic symmetry injections: While evaluating against ground truth requires controlled setups, both the 2D (MNIST/FashionMNIST) and 3D (GEOM-QM9) experiments rely on artificially sampled rotation distributions applied by the authors. Evaluating on naturally occurring unconstrained poses or real partial pose distributions would provide stronger evidence of real-world applicability.

Limited comparative baselines: The paper positions itself against SGM (Allingham et al., 2024), VP G-CNNs (Kim et al., 2024), and other symmetry-learning frameworks in Section 4, but quantitative comparisons in the main experiments are almost exclusively against the vanilla IE-AE backbone rather than competing symmetry-learning/discovery algorithms.

Multi-stage pipeline and training overhead: The entire workflow requires multiple decoupled stages (training the IE-AE backbone, performing k-NN search across the entire training dataset to calculate pseudo-labels, and then training two auxiliary equivariant/invariant networks Θ and Λ). As reported, training takes multiple days on an A100 GPU for 3D data.

Modest improvement on 3D downstream classification: On GEOM-QM9 (Figure 6d), test-time canonicalization improves accuracy only from 52.40% to 55.70%, leaving a wide gap to the 97.01% upper bound reported in Table 1.

strengths: Clear conceptual motivation: The paper identifies a pervasive and well-known issue in class-pose decomposition frameworks (such as Invariant-Equivariant Autoencoders), namely that canonical representations are arbitrarily oriented and often out-of-distribution. Normalizing canonical orientations to align with data distributions is an intuitive and sensible objective.

Sound theoretical formulation: The use of the Fréchet mean on Lie groups to estimate canonical offsets, accompanied by convergence analysis in Wasserstein distance (Proposition 3.1) and the robust Tukey-Fréchet extension for multimodal distributions, is mathematically well-grounded.

Extension beyond 2D: Unlike much prior work on symmetry learning that focuses exclusively on 2D images, this work successfully scales the formulation to SO(3) rotations on 3D geometric graphs (molecular conformers from GEOM-QM9) using steerable E(3)-equivariant networks.

Practical utility: The downstream demonstrations in test-time canonicalization (granting rotational invariance to pre-trained frozen backbones without retraining) and out-of-distribution pose detection provide concrete, useful applications.
weaknesses: Synthetic experimental setups: Across all experiments (rotated MNIST, FashionMNIST, and GEOM-QM9), the underlying pose distributions are artificially synthesized by rotating data using known parametric distributions (uniform, Gaussian, and matrix-Fisher). The paper does not demonstrate symmetry discovery on naturally occurring, non-synthesized pose variations.

Limited baseline comparisons: The primary baseline evaluated quantitatively is the uncentered IE-AE backbone. SGM (Allingham et al., 2024) is discussed qualitatively, but quantitative benchmarking against existing symmetry discovery and partial equivariance frameworks (e.g., SGM, Variational Partial G-CNNs, WSCNNs) on standardized metrics is absent.

Heavy multi-stage pipeline: The overall framework requires training an IE-AE first, extracting latent codes and running k-NN searches to compute empirical Fréchet means, and then training two additional neural networks (Theta and Lambda) on the resulting pseudo-labels. This multi-step process introduces substantial computational overhead (e.g., several days of GPU training) and error propagation risks.

Dependence on latent space separation and parametric distribution forms: The approach heavily relies on the assumption that the invariant latent space perfectly clusters identical classes/shapes via k-NN. Furthermore, learning the parameter predictor Theta requires pre-specifying a parametric distribution family, which limits applicability to complex or arbitrary real-world symmetry distributions.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Addressing the arbitrary canonical pose in class-pose decomposition methods (such as IE-AEs) is an important and recognized problem that directly hinders interpretability and test-time canonicalization.

Sound mathematical foundation: The paper provides a clear theoretical justification (Proposition 3.1) proving that right-multiplication by the empirical Fréchet mean consistently recovers the data-aligned reference pose in Wasserstein distance. The introduction of the robust Tukey-Fréchet mean to handle multimodal pose distributions is technically thoughtful.

First extension to 3D symmetry discovery: Moving beyond toy 2D image rotations to SO(3) rotations on 3D geometric graphs (GEOM-QM9 molecular conformations) represents a notable and non-trivial extension compared to existing symmetry discovery literature.

Practical downstream applications: The demonstrations on out-of-distribution (OOD) pose detection and training-free test-time canonicalization for frozen backbones show clear practical utility without requiring model retraining.
weaknesses: Reliance on synthetic rotation distributions: For both 2D (MNIST/FashionMNIST) and 3D (GEOM-QM9), the pose distributions are synthetically injected (uniform/Gaussian in 2D, Matrix-Fisher in 3D) onto pre-aligned base data. Evaluating on data with naturally occurring unaligned poses (e.g., cryo-EM images or uncurated 3D scans) would substantially strengthen the empirical claims.

Multi-stage training pipeline complexity: The full framework requires: (1) training an IE-AE; (2) performing kNN retrieval across the dataset in the invariant latent space Z; (3) computing Fréchet means and fitting distribution parameters to generate pseudo-labels; and (4) training two additional networks (Theta and Lambda) for hundreds of epochs (costing over a week on an A100 GPU for GEOM).

Sensitivity to invariant latent clustering: The method relies heavily on the assumption that semantic classes form well-separated clusters in latent space Z. While hit rates on GEOM-QM9 are high, performance in settings with continuous class variations or severe within-class structural deformations could degrade if kNN captures mixed semantic classes.

Limited comparative baselines in quantitative benchmarks: Downstream tasks (OOD pose detection and test-time canonicalization) are only compared against uncentered IE-AE and no-canonicalization. Comparing against other symmetry discovery or test-time canonicalization methods (e.g., SGM, learned frame-averaging, or canonicalization baselines like Kaba et al., 2023) would provide a stronger benchmark.
